items.title: Shift left
items.context: Shifting left means catching security issues early — in the IDE, at pull request time and in CI — where they're cheapest to fix, instead of in a final audit before release.

questions.prompt: Which is an example of shifting security left?
choices: Adding a firewall rule in production
Running dependency and SAST scans on every pull request
questions.explanation: Pen tests still matter, but they shouldn't be the first time anyone looks.

items.title: SAST, DAST, SCA
items.context: SAST analyses source code without running it (e.g. SQL injection patterns). DAST probes the running application from outside, like an attacker. SCA (software composition analysis) checks third-party dependencies for known CVEs and licence issues.

questions.prompt: Which tool type flags a vulnerable version of log4j in your dependencies?
questions.explanation: Dependabot, Snyk and OWASP Dependency-Check are SCA tools.

items.title: Leaked secrets
items.context: Once a secret has been committed and pushed, assume it's compromised: rotate or revoke it immediately. Rewriting Git history doesn't help — clones, forks, CI logs and bots may already have it. Prevent leaks with pre-commit hooks and secret scanning.

questions.prompt: You pushed an AWS access key to a public repository 2 minutes ago. First action:
choices: Revoke and rotate the key now
Wait to see if it gets used
Make the repo private and do nothing else
Rewrite history with git filter-repo and carry on
questions.explanation: Bots scrape public repos for keys within minutes. Clean the history afterwards.

items.title: Secrets managers
items.context: Store secrets in a dedicated manager (HashiCorp Vault, AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault) with access control, audit logs and rotation. Vault can issue dynamic, short-lived credentials (e.g. a database user valid for one hour) so there's no long-lived password to leak.

questions.prompt: What's the advantage of dynamic secrets?
choices: Credentials are short-lived and unique per consumer, so a leak expires quickly
They make the app run faster
They never need a network connection
questions.explanation: Revocation is per lease, and audit logs show exactly who used what.

items.title: Container image security
items.context: Scan images for CVEs (Trivy, Grype) in CI and in the registry. Use minimal base images (distroless, alpine, slim) to shrink the attack surface, run as a non-root user, and rebuild regularly to pick up patched base layers.

questions.prompt: Your image has 200 CVEs, mostly in OS packages your Java app never uses. Best first step:
choices: Switch to a minimal runtime base image (e.g. distroless or JRE-slim)
questions.explanation: Fewer packages, fewer vulnerabilities to triage.

items.title: Software supply chain
items.context: Protect the path from code to production: pin dependency versions and verify checksums, generate an SBOM (a software bill of materials, e.g. CycloneDX or SPDX), sign images and verify signatures at deploy time (Sigstore/cosign), and build in isolated, reproducible pipelines (SLSA levels).

questions.prompt: What does an SBOM give you?
choices: An inventory of every component and version in an artifact
questions.explanation: When the next log4shell drops, you can answer 'are we affected?' in minutes.

items.title: Kubernetes network policies
items.context: By default every Pod can talk to every other Pod. NetworkPolicies (enforced by a CNI such as Calico or Cilium) restrict traffic; a common baseline is default-deny for a namespace, then explicitly allow the flows that are needed.

questions.prompt: A good baseline for a sensitive namespace is:
choices: Default-deny ingress, then allow specific flows
Give every Pod a public IP
questions.explanation: This limits lateral movement if one Pod is compromised.

items.title: Policy as code
items.context: Policy engines such as OPA Gatekeeper and Kyverno check resources against rules at admission time — e.g. reject Pods running as root, images not from the company registry, or missing resource limits. Tools like Checkov and tfsec do the same for Terraform plans in CI.

questions.prompt: How can you automatically reject Kubernetes Pods that run as root?
choices: An admission policy (Kyverno or OPA Gatekeeper)
questions.explanation: Policies are versioned and reviewed like any other code.

items.title: Keyless CI credentials
items.context: Instead of storing cloud access keys as CI secrets, use OIDC federation: the CI system (e.g. GitHub Actions) issues a short-lived signed token for the job, and the cloud exchanges it for temporary credentials tied to a role, restricted to a specific repository and branch.

questions.prompt: Main benefit of OIDC federation from CI to the cloud:
choices: No long-lived cloud keys are stored in CI
questions.explanation: Credentials last minutes and can be limited to, say, the main branch of one repo.

items.title: OWASP Top 10
items.context: The OWASP Top 10 lists the most critical web application risks. In the 2021 edition, Broken Access Control is #1, followed by Cryptographic Failures and Injection.

questions.prompt: Which risk is #1 in the OWASP Top 10 (2021)?
questions.explanation: XSS is now grouped under Injection (#3).

items.title: Least privilege
items.context: Give every identity — human, service, CI job — only the permissions it needs, for only as long as it needs them. Scope by resource and action, review regularly, and prefer short-lived credentials.

questions.prompt: A deploy job only updates one ECS service. Its IAM role should allow:
choices: Full S3 access just in case
All ECS actions in every account
questions.explanation: If the job is compromised, the damage stays small.

items.title: mTLS
items.context: Mutual TLS makes both sides present certificates, so services authenticate each other, not just the server. Service meshes (Istio, Linkerd) can enable mTLS between all Pods automatically.

questions.prompt: What does mTLS add over regular TLS?
choices: The client also authenticates with a certificate
questions.explanation: It's a building block of zero-trust networking inside clusters.

items.title: Web Application Firewall
items.context: A WAF filters HTTP traffic in front of an application, blocking common attacks (SQL injection, XSS patterns, bad bots) and rate-limiting abusive clients. It reduces risk, but doesn't replace fixing the vulnerabilities in code.

questions.prompt: A WAF is best described as:
choices: An extra layer that filters malicious HTTP requests
questions.explanation: Defence in depth: fix the code and filter the traffic.

items.title: Hardening containers
items.context: Run containers as a non-root user, with a read-only root filesystem, all Linux capabilities dropped except those needed, no privilege escalation (allowPrivilegeEscalation: false), and never privileged: true unless truly unavoidable.

questions.prompt: Which securityContext setting is a red flag?
questions.explanation: Privileged containers get nearly full access to the host.

items.title: Pod Security Standards
items.context: Kubernetes defines three Pod Security Standards — privileged (unrestricted), baseline (blocks known privilege escalations) and restricted (hardened best practice) — enforced per namespace by the built-in Pod Security Admission via labels.

questions.prompt: Which level should most application namespaces aim for?
questions.explanation: baseline is a stepping stone when restricted isn't yet possible.

items.title: Encryption at rest and in transit
items.context: Encryption in transit (TLS) protects data moving over networks; encryption at rest (disk, database or object encryption with managed keys) protects stored data if media or backups leak. You usually need both.

questions.prompt: Enabling HTTPS on your API protects data:
questions.explanation: Database and disk encryption cover data at rest.

items.title: Secret scanning
items.context: Tools such as gitleaks, trufflehog and GitHub secret scanning detect keys and tokens in commits. Run them as pre-commit hooks and in CI so secrets are caught before they're pushed.

questions.prompt: Where should secret scanning run to stop leaks earliest?
choices: In a pre-commit hook (and again in CI)
questions.explanation: Push protection on the hosting platform adds another net.

items.title: Zero trust
items.context: Zero trust drops the idea of a trusted internal network: every request is authenticated, authorised and encrypted based on identity and context, whether it comes from the office, a VPN or the internet.

questions.prompt: Under zero trust, a request from inside the corporate network is:
choices: Verified just like any other request
questions.explanation: Identity replaces network location as the boundary.

items.title: Triaging vulnerabilities
items.context: Scanners flag far more CVEs than you can fix at once. Prioritise by severity (CVSS) combined with real risk: is it exploitable (known exploits, the EPSS score), is the vulnerable code reachable, is the service internet-facing? Fix critical, reachable, exposed issues first.

questions.prompt: Which CVE do you patch first?
choices: A low-severity issue in a test-only dependency
A high-severity, actively exploited flaw in an internet-facing service
A critical CVE in a library function your code never calls, in an offline batch tool
questions.explanation: Severity alone isn't priority; exploitability and exposure matter.
